chapter: History III · The Making of a Global World
source: NCERT India and the Contemporary World II (Class X History), Chapter III

overview.bigIdea: Globalisation is not new. For centuries **trade, migration and capital** have linked the world – through silk routes, conquest and disease, colonial plantations, two world wars, a Great Depression and the Bretton Woods system. Each phase brought **growth for some and misery for others**.

plan.text: Lesson 1 – silk routes, food, conquest and disease.
Lessons 2–3 – three flows, Corn Laws chain, rinderpest, indenture, India’s trade.
Lesson 4 – war, Ford, Depression and India.
Lesson 5, then the quiz; revise after 1, 3 and 7 days.

lessons.title: The pre-modern world
lessons.hook: Your potato, tomato and chilli are travellers. Until about **500 years ago** nobody in India or Europe had tasted them – they came from the Americas after Columbus.

core.def: Indus valley–West Asia coastal trade (3000 BCE); Maldives cowries to China and East Africa; germs spread from the 7th century.

Land and sea routes linking Asia, Europe and northern Africa; Chinese silk and pottery, Indian and Southeast Asian textiles and spices; gold and silver flowed east; Buddhism, Christianity and Islam spread.
Noodles → spaghetti (perhaps); potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies, sweet potatoes from America; Irish Potato Famine 1845–49.
Portuguese and Spanish conquest of America by mid-16th century; smallpox killed natives who had no immunity; silver from Peru and Mexico.
China retreated into isolation from the 15th century; Americas rose; Europe became the centre of world trade.

explain: **Indian Ocean:** for centuries a bustling trade with the subcontinent at its centre; Europeans expanded or redirected flows towards Europe.
**Slavery:** by the 18th century plantations in America, worked by slaves captured in Africa, grew cotton and sugar for European markets.

example.q: Explain how the global transfer of disease in the pre-modern world helped in the colonisation of the Americas. (3 marks)
steps: **Isolation:** America’s original inhabitants had been cut off for millions of years and had no immunity to European diseases.
**Smallpox:** carried by Spanish conquerors, it spread deep into the continent, even ahead of Europeans.
**Result:** it killed and decimated whole communities, paving the way for conquest – guns could be captured, but not diseases.
example.answer: No immunity → smallpox spread → communities destroyed → conquest.

mistakes: Saying potatoes are native to India.
Saying superior firepower alone won America.
Forgetting that gold and silver flowed FROM Europe TO Asia on the silk routes.
lessons.tip: ‘Two examples of global exchange before the 17th century’: one from Asia (silk routes) and one from the Americas (food crops or smallpox).
lessons.memory: 3000 BCE Indus–West Asia · Silk routes till ~15th c. · Potatoes after Columbus · Smallpox = weapon · Irish famine 1845–49.
examAsk: Give two examples of global exchange before the 17th century.
How did disease help colonise the Americas?
What do we mean when we say the world ‘shrank’ in the 1500s?

play.title: What travelled where?
play.say: Tap the direction in which each item moved.
items: Introduced to Europe and Asia after Columbus.
Gave the silk routes their name.
Paid for Asian goods on the silk routes.

lessons.title: A world economy takes shape (1815–1914)
lessons.hook: In 1890 a Londoner’s bread came from wheat grown thousands of miles away by a recently arrived worker on a farm that was a forest a generation ago – carried by a railway built just for it.

core.def: Trade (goods like cloth or wheat), labour (migration for work), capital (short- or long-term investment over long distances).
Restricted corn imports under pressure from landed groups; abolished after industrialists and urban dwellers objected.
Nearly 50 million left Europe for America and Australia; about 150 million worldwide.
Multiplied 25–40 times, 1820–1914; nearly 60% primary products.
Railways, steamships, telegraph; refrigerated ships for frozen meat.
West Punjab irrigated for wheat and cotton exports, settled by peasants from other parts of Punjab.

explain: **Corn Laws chain:** abolition → cheap imports → British farming collapses → unemployed go to cities or abroad → food prices fall, demand rises → lands cleared in Eastern Europe, Russia, America, Australia → railways, ports, settlements need capital (London) and labour (migrants).
**Meat:** before the 1870s live animals were shipped – costly, many died. Refrigerated ships made meat cheap: Europe’s poor added meat, butter and eggs to bread and potatoes.

example.q: Explain the effects of the British government’s decision to abolish the Corn Laws. (3 marks)
steps: **Cheap imports:** food could be imported more cheaply than it was produced in Britain.
**Rural crisis:** British agriculture could not compete; land lay uncultivated; thousands lost work and moved to cities or overseas.
**Global change:** as food prices fell and demand rose, lands were cleared abroad, and capital and labour flowed to America and Australia.
example.answer: Cheap food → farm collapse → migration → world agricultural economy.

mistakes: Saying the Corn Laws were abolished by landlords (industrialists and urban dwellers forced it).
Saying technology alone caused change (it was shaped by social and political factors).
lessons.tip: Draw the Corn Laws flow chart with 5 arrows – the textbook asks for it as an activity and it scores well in long answers.
lessons.memory: 3 flows: Trade · Labour · Capital · 50 million emigrants · Trade ×25–40 · 60% primary · Refrigerated ships.
examAsk: Explain the three types of flows with examples involving India.
Effects of abolishing the Corn Laws.
Give two examples of the impact of technology on food availability.

cards.q: What made frozen meat exports possible?

play.title: The Corn Laws flow chart
play.say: Tap each step of the chain in order.
items: British farming cannot compete; workers lose jobs
Food prices fall and consumption rises
Lands cleared in America, Russia and Australia
Capital flows from London and labour migrates
play.done: Britain’s decision to import food led to migration to America and Australia.

lessons.title: Colonialism, rinderpest, indenture and Indian trade
lessons.hook: In the 1890s a cattle disease raced across Africa ‘like forest fire’ and killed **90%** of the cattle. For European colonisers it was the tool that finally forced Africans to work for wages.

core.def: Britain and France expanded; Belgium and Germany new colonial powers; US took Spanish colonies; Berlin 1885 carved up Africa.
Came in the late 1880s with infected cattle from British Asia for Italian soldiers in Eritrea; Atlantic coast 1892; Cape five years later; 90% cattle killed.
Heavy taxes payable only by wage work; inheritance laws changed; miners confined in compounds; control of scarce cattle.
Five-year contracts; from eastern UP, Bihar, central India, dry Tamil Nadu; to Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam, Mauritius, Fiji; ‘a new system of slavery’; abolished 1921.
Shikaripuri Shroffs, Nattukottai Chettiars; Hyderabadi Sindhi traders’ emporia from the 1860s.
Cotton textiles fell from ~30% of exports (1800) to 15% (1815) to below 3% (1870s); raw cotton rose 5% → 35% (1812–1871); opium to China; trade surplus paid home charges.

explain: **Culture of survival:** Hosay in Trinidad, Rastafarianism, chutney music – cultural fusion is part of the making of the global world.

**Multilateral settlement:** Britain’s surplus with India balanced its deficits with other countries; it also paid ‘home charges’ – remittances, interest on India’s debt and pensions of British officials.

example.q: Explain the effects of the coming of rinderpest to Africa. (3/5 marks)
steps: **Before:** land and livestock sustained Africans; few worked for wages.
**Spread:** entered East Africa in the late 1880s, reached the Atlantic coast in 1892 and the Cape five years later.
**Destruction:** killed 90 per cent of the cattle and destroyed African livelihoods.
**Monopoly:** planters, mine owners and colonial governments took control of scarce cattle.
**Result:** Africans were forced into the labour market; Europeans could conquer and subdue Africa.
example.answer: Livelihood lost → cattle monopolised → forced labour → conquest.

mistakes: Saying indentured workers mostly returned to India (most stayed).
Saying India exported more cotton cloth in the 19th century (it exported raw cotton).
lessons.tip: For indenture letters or answers use: recruitment (agents, false promises) → journey → harsh work and punishment → cultural survival.
lessons.memory: Berlin 1885 · Rinderpest 90% · 1892 Atlantic · Indenture 5 years, abolished 1921 · Cotton cloth 30% → <3% · Raw cotton 5% → 35%.
examAsk: Imagine you are an indentured labourer – write a letter home.
How did India help Britain balance its trade?

play.title: Colonial connections
play.say: Match each item with what it explains.

Trinidad carnival from the Muharram procession

lessons.title: The inter-war economy and the Great Depression
lessons.hook: Cars rolled off Henry Ford’s line every **three minutes** and Americans bought fridges on hire purchase. Then in 1929 it all vanished ‘in a puff of dust’.

core.def: Allies (Britain, France, Russia, later US) vs Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman Turkey); first modern industrial war; 9 million dead, 20 million injured; women took men’s jobs; US became a creditor.
Lost Indian market to Indian and Japanese industry; huge debts; 1921 – one in five workers jobless.
Ford’s assembly line (from a Chicago slaughterhouse) in Detroit; $5 wage (1914); unions banned; T-Model; US car output 2 million (1919) → 5 million+ (1929); hire purchase.
Agricultural overproduction and falling prices; withdrawal of US loans (over $1 billion in early 1928 to a quarter a year later); US doubled import duties.
Over 4,000 banks closed by 1933; about 110,000 companies collapsed 1929–32.
Exports and imports nearly halved 1928–34; wheat prices fell 50%; jute price crashed over 60%; revenue not cut; gold exported; urban fixed-income groups better off.

explain: **Wheat glut:** eastern Europe’s supply returned after the war while Canada, America and Australia had expanded – prices fell and farmers fell into debt.
**Link to India’s politics:** rural India was seething with unrest when Gandhiji launched Civil Disobedience at the height of the Depression.

example.q: Explain the causes of the Great Depression. (5 marks)
steps: **Fragile post-war economy:** the war boom ended and recovery was difficult.
**Agricultural overproduction:** falling prices made farmers grow more, worsening the glut; farm produce rotted.
**Dependence on US loans:** many countries financed investment with US loans; lenders panicked – loans fell from over $1 billion (first half of 1928) to a quarter of that a year later.
**Spread:** bank failures and currency collapse in Europe; slump in agricultural and raw material prices in Latin America.
**Protectionism:** the US doubled import duties, a severe blow to world trade; US banks called back loans and collapsed.
example.answer: Overproduction + loan withdrawal + protectionism = worldwide slump.

mistakes: Saying the Depression began in India.
Saying Ford raised wages out of kindness (he called it his best cost-cutting decision).
Forgetting that urban India was less hurt.
lessons.tip: India and the Depression: Trade halved, Wheat −50%, Jute −60%, Revenue unchanged, Gold exported, Cities better off.
lessons.memory: WWI 9m dead · Ford $5 (1914) · Cars 2m → 5m · 1929 crash · 4,000 banks · India wheat −50%, jute −60%.
examAsk: Explain the causes of the Great Depression.
Effects of the Great Depression on the Indian economy.
Effects of the death of working-age men in Europe in the war.

play.title: Who was hit hardest?
play.say: Decide whether each group suffered or was better off in India during the Depression.
items: Peasants producing for the world market

lessons.title: Rebuilding the world economy after 1945
lessons.hook: In July 1944, while war still raged, delegates met at a hotel in **Bretton Woods** to design a world economy that would never collapse like 1929 again.

core.def: Axis (Germany, Japan, Italy) vs Allies (Britain, France, Soviet Union, US); at least 60 million dead (~3% of 1939 population); more civilians than soldiers died.
Mass production needs mass consumption → stable incomes → full employment, ensured by government; governments must control flows of goods, capital and labour.
IMF (external surpluses and deficits) and World Bank (reconstruction) – the Bretton Woods twins; operations from 1947; US effective veto; fixed exchange rates; dollar = $35 per ounce of gold.
World trade grew over 8% a year and incomes nearly 5% (1950–70); unemployment under 5%.
New nations poor; IMF/World Bank turned to them from the late 1950s; G-77 demanded NIEO.
Dollar lost confidence → floating rates; developing countries borrowed from commercial banks → debt crises; MNCs moved to low-wage Asia (China); India, China, Brazil transformed.

explain: **Two dominant powers:** the US in the Western world and the Soviet Union, which had transformed itself into a world power during the Depression years.
**MNCs:** large companies operating in many countries; spread in the 1950s–60s partly because high tariffs forced them to become ‘domestic producers’.

example.q: What is meant by the Bretton Woods Agreement? (3 marks)
steps: **Conference:** UN Monetary and Financial Conference, July 1944, Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA – aim: economic stability and full employment in the industrial world.
**Institutions:** IMF to deal with members’ external surpluses and deficits; World Bank to finance post-war reconstruction.
**System:** fixed exchange rates – national currencies pegged to the dollar, the dollar anchored to gold at $35 per ounce.

mistakes: Saying the IMF was set up to help colonies (it was designed for industrial countries).
Mixing fixed and floating exchange rates.
Saying the G-77 is a group of rich countries.
lessons.tip: G-77 answers: who (developing countries), why (did not benefit, controlled by former colonial powers), what (NIEO – four demands).
lessons.memory: WWII 60m · Bretton Woods July 1944 · IMF + World Bank (1947) · $35/oz · Trade +8% · G-77 → NIEO · MNCs to low-wage Asia.
examAsk: What is meant by the Bretton Woods Agreement?
Explain the G-77 and its link to the Bretton Woods twins.
Effects of MNCs relocating production to Asia.

play.title: From war to globalisation
items: 1947 – IMF and World Bank begin operations
Late 1950s – Bretton Woods institutions turn to developing countries
From the 1960s – US dollar loses confidence; fixed rates give way to floating rates
Mid-1970s – developing countries forced to borrow from Western commercial banks
Late 1970s – MNCs shift production to low-wage Asian countries
play.done: Bretton Woods → its twins → turn to developing countries → floating rates → debt → globalisation.

formulas.name: Silk routes
formulas.f: Asia–Europe–N. Africa, before the Christian Era to ~15th c.

revision: Global links are old: Indus–West Asia trade (3000 BCE), Maldives cowries, silk routes.
Food travelled: potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies from America; Irish Potato Famine 1845–49.
Smallpox helped Spanish conquest of America; silver from Peru and Mexico enriched Europe.
Corn Laws abolished → cheap imports → British farming declined → migration and global agriculture; ~50 million left Europe.
World trade ×25–40 (1820–1914), 60% primary products; refrigerated ships cut meat prices.
Berlin 1885 carved up Africa; rinderpest killed 90% cattle and forced Africans into wage labour.
Indenture: 5 years; eastern UP, Bihar, central India, Tamil Nadu → Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji; abolished 1921.
Indian bankers abroad: Shikaripuri Shroffs, Nattukottai Chettiars; Hyderabadi Sindhi traders.
India: cotton cloth exports fell (30% → <3%), raw cotton rose (5% → 35%); opium to China; surplus paid home charges.
WWI: first industrial war; 9 million dead; US becomes creditor; Britain in debt; 1921 one in five unemployed.
Ford’s assembly line, $5 wage, mass consumption on hire purchase.
Depression (1929): overproduction, US loan withdrawal, US import duties; India – trade halved, wheat −50%, jute −60%.
Bretton Woods (1944): IMF, World Bank; fixed rates; dollar at $35/oz gold.
G-77 demanded NIEO; fixed rates collapsed; MNCs moved to low-wage Asia.

sections.title: Cause–effect answers · 4 steps
items: Name the event and its date.
Follow the chain to the wider effect (flow chart).
Say who gained and who lost.

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line introduction using the textbook’s key term (e.g. ‘Proto-industrialisation was …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, key term first. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a date, a name or a figure from the chapter to each point – but only when you are sure of it.
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Compare’ draw a small two-column table.
Source-based questions: underline the key line in the source first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn timelines and sorts – if you get every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can give examples of pre-modern global exchange from Asia and the Americas.
I can explain the three flows and the Corn Laws chain.
I can explain rinderpest, indenture and India’s role in the world economy.
I can explain the First World War’s effects and the causes of the Great Depression.
I can describe the Depression’s impact on India.
I can explain Bretton Woods, G-77 and the start of globalisation.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark source-based and 5-mark long answers; History also has map work). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
